notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 1 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

Congratulations on entering the Bouddi 21km event. Here is some information to help you decide which level of the plan will make you the fittest, fastest and strongest on race day.

We have three different volume/difficulty levels of our Bouddi 21k Training Program. They are a reflection on how much time you have available to train, rather than a reflection on your goal time for the event. Some runners will be able to complete 21km in <2 hours following the intermediate plan, and other runners might take >3 hours following the advanced plan.

You need to choose a level that you feel will be sustainable for the entire 12-week program. Your body needs to be able to comfortably cope with the volume without causing you illness or injuries, and your training schedule needs to be able to fit around all of the other aspects of your day-to-day life, such as work and family commitments.

You don’t have to stick to the same level for the entire plan (you have access to all three levels), you can go up or down levels depending on your time availability and how your body is coping with the volume. The key is consistency. You need to choose the level that allows you to run every week without needing any enforced rest.

Read the description in the Glossary Tab to decide whether you should follow the beginner, intermediate or advanced plan.

Stretching, Rolling and Strength

This week we are introducing a 3 minute morning stretching routine that you will be doing most days during the plan. This short and easy routine helps to stretch your lower back, glutes, quads, hip flexors, hips, knees, ankles and calf muscles. It will help you to remain injury free – so please try and stick with it every day you see it in the plan.

We are also introducing two different 10 minute bodyweight strength and stability routines (no equipment needed) and a 5 minute foam rolling and massage ball routine. To perform this you will need a foam roller and some sort of firm massage ball.

Training Plan

Make Sure You “Listen to your body”

This is an age-old cliché, but it has stood the test of time for good reason. It works! If something hurts when you are running, then don’t ignore it. Especially if it lingers for more than a few days. If possible, get it diagnosed by a health professional who runs. No one understands a runner’s body (and psyche) as well as a fellow runner. You will be able to resume training much quicker if you understand your injury and know what you can be doing to help your recovery

Do not try and stick to the weekly km if you do have an issue. Continuing to push through pain when you have a problem could stop you turning up on race day.

How to Use the Plan

To use the program properly, and to get the most benefit from it, you need to understand what all the session descriptions mean, so that you can use them to best effect in your training. You will see a number of shorthand descriptions which describe the particulars for that specific run. For example “Hill Reps” or “ELEV” or “UpDown Reps”

Go to the Glossary Tab for a detailed description of each training session

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

You need to start by working on the absolute foundation of what will lead to a successful race. Your running technique. It doesn’t matter how many stretches or exercises you do, if your running technique is not up to scratch, you will be much more likely to suffer a number of common running injuries and you will never reach your full potential.

Watch this video to learn how to run with good technique.

Strength Vs Stability

To be able to run and avoid injuries, you need to have good hip and pelvis stability. When working properly, the role of the stability muscles is to stabilise your skeleton and spine in the optimal position so the bigger, stronger muscles can develop force and create movement.

The ability to stand on one foot with your eyes closed for 60 seconds requires you to have good stability – We are going to test this in a minute .

I have often seen clients who can squat 100kg, or perform 100 sit-ups, but if they can’t stand on one foot for a minute, then the relative strength of their “movement” muscles is not going to help their running performance.

Test Your Stability Now

To get an understanding of stability, I want you to do this simple one minute test. Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Start counting in seconds 1, 2, 3…………

How long did you last until you had to put your foot down?.

If you made it to

- less than 10… You have a lot of work to do

- 10 – 30 ……. Still not good. Your lack of hip stability might cause some injuries

- 30 – 45 …….. Better, but still room for improvement

- 60 seconds …….. Great. Keep doing what you are doing

Record your results because we are going to test this again later in the plan

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
We have put together an awesome weekly guide on how to manage your food and hydration during training and for race day. Nailing your nutrition is equally as important as following the training and recovery sessions, so I urge you to follow this advice.

This week, the focus is on “Just Eat Real Food”

Following the “JERF” principle is an excellent way to guide your meal and snack choices – it is also referred to as a “whole foods” diet.

This is food that comes out of the ground, off a tree or from an animal – and that has been processed minimally – if at all.

This will provide you with a very nutrient dense diet and will make a significant impact on your overall health and wellbeing. Not only due to the nutrients that you are putting in, but also due to what you are leaving out. Packaged foods most often contain highly refined vegetables oils, chemicals, flavour enhancers, preservatives and refined sugars – which all play havoc with your liver, metabolism and hormones.

The foods you choose provide the body with the building blocks and nutrients it requires for cell growth and DNA replication – this has a direct impact on your muscles, ligaments, immune system and vitality. Quality of food is as important as the quality of training and rest – these 3 combined is what influences your performance and recovery.

…. “you are what you eat”

Your homework this week.

The single biggest thing you can do to improve your nutrition is meal planning. If you have good food ready and available in the fridge you are 90% there.

Being organised and planning ahead is critical – shopping, preparing and some cooking. Allocate a couple of hours on the weekend or one evening to write down the next few days meals, and then shop accordingly – online and delivery services make this even easier

Jot down your meals for the week and see if you can make some healthy improvements to your diet.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 2 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

I hope you enjoyed your first week on the training plan. The first week included an overview into how to improve your running technique, some exercises to improve your core stability and we also introduced the 3 minute morning ritual.

Trail Vs Road – Do you have to do your long run on a trail?

I appreciate that not everyone will be able to run on a trail for all of their runs. Practice makes perfect. The best thing you can do to make yourself a stronger trail runner and to enjoy your race, is to run on trails which are similar to the terrain you expect to encounter on race day. Start doing some research now on your chosen event and try to find similar trails to train on.

If you find it difficult to get to a trail every weekend, you should try and plan a road route with a lot of hills, some stairs if possible, and mix up the terrain as much as possible e.g. road, grass, footpath, gravel etc.

What if you live in a flat area?

Are you training for a hilly trail event but you live on the flat? or you generally just struggle to find enough hills or stairs to train on? This is a common problem faced by runners, and it can cause quite a few issues on race day. Mostly cramping in the calves, hamstrings and adductor muscles.

Watch THIS VIDEO to learn how to use a Lunge-Squat-Lunge-Run Session is an easy way to help strengthen your legs for uphills, downhills and stairs no matter where you live. The idea is to use lunges and squats to increase the load on your leg muscles and also to get your joints and muscles working through a bigger range of motion. You then run 1km and repeat the squats and lunges – multiple times.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

Have you started to focus on your running technique yet? The sooner you learn to run with good technique the better. It is a VITAL component in the quest to staying injury free, and running faster.

In the video I refer to the importance of “cadence”. Cadence is the number of steps per minute you take when you are running. Running with the correct cadence is integral to good running form, and therefore also integral to staying injury-free. We will talk more about this as the weeks progress.

Uphill Running Technique

“Rolling Hills” feature a lot in this program, so now is the perfect time to learn how to run uphills efficiently.

Rolling hills is the term we use to describe running over a course that is consistently going up and downhill for the duration of your run. Plan ahead and identify a course that has a good amount of up and downhill. The hills don’t have to be steep but they should be as regular as possible throughout the course. Consider running a short hilly loop multiple times if you don’t have access to a long hilly route. You should average approximately 150m – 250m of vertical elevation per 10km of running on rolling hills.

The better your form when you run up the hills the faster you will be and the more energy you will conserve for later in the race.

Watch this video to learn what to focus on every time you are running uphill.

Accelerations

This week we are adding accelerations to the program. Accelerations are 20 to 40 second efforts building from an easy jog to a relaxed hard effort, and then easing back down to a jog again. Focus on running tall and keeping your cadence high and your strides short. Slowly walk or jog for 1 minute between accelerations. The purpose of accelerations is improve your leg speed, hip mobility, glute strength and your running technique. NB: They are not a sprinting or speed work session.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Do you stick to a weekly food plan? Planning your food in advance will certainly help you make better food choices. Nutrition is a critical part of your training and helps your body recover and get stronger.

This week we are covering the important role of carbohydrates in your training.

Carbohydrates are your body’s preferred source of energy. They are the backbone of an endurance athlete’s diet.

Your body turns carbohydrates into glucose (energy). The brain requires a significant amount of glucose (or energy) to operate efficiently, maintain concentration, avoid mood swings and avoid sugar cravings.

Intake needs to be adjusted depending on expected energy output / activity level – as only a finite amount of carbohydrates can be used as fuel or stored as glycogen, with any left over carbohydrate potentially being stored as fat.

Excess carbohydrates can cause the body to make too much insulin leading to high blood sugar levels and then rapid decreases – or fluctuating energy levels ( 3pm slump anyone? ). This happens more often when simple, processed carbohydrates are being consumed instead of complex carbohydrates.

So what should you eat and how much is enough?

Most people following an ultra marathon training program will need between 3-6 grams of carbs per kilo of body weight per day.

For example a 70kg athlete may have anywhere from 210gms carbs per day to 420gms per day – it is a large variation… as it depends on body type and exercise load.

The majority of carbs should be whole unrefined complex carbohydrates ie vegetables, fruit and whole grains.

However, not all are created equal – so it is important to understand the carbohydrate load of different fruit, vegetables and grains.

For example – starchy carbs are much higher in carbohydrate load – this includes vegetables that grow below the ground like potato and sweet potato, also grains such as oats, corn, rice, quinoa, and legumes, beans and peas.

If your goal is to reduce your weight then it is best to avoid too many of these starchy carbs – or only have them as part of your post training meal. I will cover this in detail in the coming weeks.

This week, I want you to stick with following your JERF ( just eat real food) plan from last week. Try and make it more of a habit

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 3 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

This week we have some Stair Reps. For these stair repeats, you need to find the longest convenient staircase that you can. The more steps the better. You will get the most benefit from hiking them rather than running them. You use your calf, glute and quads muscles in a slightly different way when you are hiking, and you need to train them to be strong at hiking. There are a lot of stairs in the Bouddi 21km event and it will probably be more efficient to hike them than to run them. If you hike the stairs you will be faster on the runnable terrain in other parts of the course.

When doing these stair reps you can hike up and then run or walk slowly back down the stairs to recover. Repeat for the stated duration on the training plan.

Your pace for each stair rep should stay consistent throughout the session. Don’t start so fast that you can’t maintain your pace.

A recap from last week:

What if you live in a flat area?

Are you training for a hilly trail event but you live on the flat? or you generally just struggle to find enough hills or stairs to train on? This is a common problem faced by runners, and it can cause quite a few issues on race day. Mostly cramping in the calves, hamstrings and adductor muscles.

Watch THIS VIDEO to learn how to use a Lunge-Squat-Lunge-Run Session is an easy way to help strengthen your legs for uphills, downhills and stairs no matter where you live. The idea is to use lunges and squats to increase the load on your leg muscles and also to get your joints and muscles working through a bigger range of motion. You then run 1km and repeat the squats and lunges – multiple times.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

By now your running technique should be improving and the changes you have made should be starting to feel a bit more natural.

The three most important components of running technique are:

- Posture – stand up tall

- Cadence – 175 – 185 steps/minute

- Short Strides – foot landing close to under your body

Uphill Running Technique

This week we continue to focus on “Rolling Hills” in the training program – make sure you have nailed your uphill technique so that you are fast and efficient up the hills.

Stair Running Technique

Watch this video on Stair Running Technique to learn how to run efficiently both up and down stairs. We are introducing some stair repeats into the program this week. If your chosen 21km race includes stairs then you should also try to incorporate a few stairs into your weekend long runs if possible.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
This week, we’re focusing on the importance of protein in your diet and how much you should be consuming.

Alongside healthy carbohydrates, every meal and snack should include a source of protein. Here’s why protein is essential:

- Stabilises blood sugar levels

- Prevents energy crashes and curbs constant cravings

- Promotes satiety , making you feel fuller for longer

- Provides building blocks (amino acids) for muscles, hair, nails, brain cells, and immune system cells

- Supports hormone production , including essential ones like adrenaline

Which Foods Are Rich in Protein?

Animal-Based Proteins

These provide a complete amino acid profile, making them an excellent source of protein:

- Meat : Beef, lamb, turkey, chicken, pork

- Seafood : Fish, shellfish, prawns

- Eggs : Nature’s perfect protein

- Dairy : Milk, cheese, cream, yogurt

Plant-Based Proteins

Plant proteins are often incomplete, providing only some of the essential amino acids. To ensure your body gets all it needs, pair different plant proteins together—a practice known as “food combining.”

- Nuts and Seeds : Cashews, Brazil nuts, walnuts, pumpkin seeds, hemp, sunflower seeds, sesame seeds

- Legumes and Peas : Lentils, chickpeas, lima beans, kidney beans

- Grains : Oats, wheat germ, brown rice, quinoa, buckwheat

- Soy Products : Soybeans, tofu, edamame

Including a variety of these protein sources in your diet ensures you meet your nutritional needs while supporting overall health and energy.

When should you eat protein and how much is enough?

For optimal results, include a small amount of protein in every meal and snack. Most athletes require 1.2–1.5 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight .

For example, a 70 kg athlete needs about 85–105 grams of protein daily .

Protein Content Examples

- Meat : About 25–30% protein by weight. A 100 g portion of cooked chicken provides roughly 25 g of protein.

- Eggs : One large egg contains about 8 g of protein.

How to Track Your Protein Intake

To ensure you’re meeting your daily requirements:

- Track your meals for 1–2 weeks using an app like MyFitnessPal .

- Check labels on packaged foods such as nuts, grains, and dairy to see their protein content.

Key Tips for Protein Consumption

- Distribute protein evenly throughout the day across meals and snacks.

- The body can only absorb up to 40 grams of protein at a time , so consuming a large portion (e.g., a 300 g steak) at dinner won’t maximise your intake.

- Aim for 20–30 grams per meal , with the remainder coming from snacks.

Your Homework for the Week

Set up a free account on MyFitnessPal or a similar app to log your meals. This will help you understand your eating patterns and how they impact your performance.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 4 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan – A recovery week.

Good news.

This week is a recovery week in the 12-week program, so the long run is shorter and the Thursday session is easier. By reducing the volume and intensity of the training this week, it will allow your body a chance to recover from the fatigue and tight muscles which will have been building up over the last three weeks.

The recovery week will set you up to be fresh and raring to go for the next build phase of the program.

Despite the reduced running volume, this is NOT A REST WEEK . You need to continue with the same number of runs per week and be just as diligent (if not, more so) with your body maintenance sessions.

A week of complete rest will probably leave you feeling tired and sluggish and less motivated to get back into the training next week. The aim of the recovery week is to keep your body and your brain used to running, whilst still logging some all-important km’s in the training diary.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
We have focused on running technique for the last three weeks. Make sure you keep it “front of mind” during every run. Bad habits have a tendency to start creeping in as you become fatigued. Towards the end of the long run is when you are most likely to revert back to over-striding and dropping your cadence.

One strategy to combat this drop in form is to have short walking breaks.

You might be two hours into the long run, for example, feeling tired and starting to slump down and overstride.

If you walk for a couple of minutes then start running again, you will be more likely to be able to maintain a good posture and cadence. You can have as many walking breaks as you need to throughout the run as they won’t have a negative effect on your endurance, and they will ultimately increase your chances of being able to stick with this program.

Keep this little mantra running through your head, especially when you are tired “stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall . . . “

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Last week, you should have set up an account with My Fitness Pal, or a similar app, to start tracking the amount of protein and carbohydrates you are consuming.

This week we are going to take a look at Healthy Fats – why are they important and where do they come from?

Healthy fats are essential. Healthy fats will NOT make you fat, in fact they will help you to lose weight. Healthy fats help to make you feel full and satisfied, so that you don’t over consume calories. Fat is essential for cell membranes, hormone production and also for transport and absorption of nutrients – especially vitamins A,D,E and K.

Each meal should contain a small amount of fat – this is pretty easy when you are following the “JERF” principle and hitting your protein requirement – as fat is often “packaged” with protein – as you will see from the list below.

An easy way to increase fat in your diet is to drizzle a small amount of olive oil on your vegetables and salads.

Another popular way for athletes to increase fat intake is to consume MCT oil in a coffee (it’s called “bulletproof” coffee). MCT (Medium Chain Triglyceride) is from coconut oil, and is an excellent source of healthy fat.

The human body can make most of the types of fats it needs from other fats or raw materials. However, that is not the case for omega-3 fatty acids – the body can’t make them from scratch, but must get them from food. They are therefore called Essential Fatty Acids. One of the easiest, most convenient and economical ways to increase your Omega 3 intake is to eat tinned Sardines.

A lot of people are happy to eat tinned Tuna, which provides around 150mg of Omega 3 per serve, but Sardines provide 2900mg per serve – nearly 20 times as much.

There is no set standard for how much combined EPA/DHA you need each day, although healthy experts generally recommend 250mg – 500mg per day. So one tin of tuna per day is not enough, whereas if you had tinned Sardines 2 times per week instead –you are smashing it.

Before screw up our nose and say “yuck” …. Spend the $3 and just try them …you might be surprised.

My favourite way is to have them as part of a big salad for lunch, others enjoy them on sourdough toast, or just straight from the tin as a snack.

Examples of healthy fats

- Oils – Coconut Oil, Olive Oil, Flaxseed Oil, Nut Oils

- Animal Fats – skin on chicken, lard, egg yolks

- Fatty Fish – Salmon, Mackerel and Sardines,

- Full Fat Dairy foods – choose good quality butter, yoghurt, ricotta cheese, full fat milk, cheese, haloumi

- All Nuts and Seeds – examples are cashews, brazil, walnuts, sunflower, pepitas, linseeds, chia, hemp

- Fruits – Avocado, Coconut

notes.label: Gear
notes.text:
Naked Running Band

The Naked Running Band is my favourite running accessory of all time. It can carry a lot of stuff and it works very well in tandem with a vest / pack.

Naked Running Bands are great for carrying your poles and race number, and they provide extra capacity for carrying water and food.

These bands are perfect for both training and racing.

I can comfortably carry 1 litre of water, my phone, a snake bandage, a survival blanket and a bunch of gels without the band bouncing, and without the need for training with a vest / pack. I use this on training runs and shorter races.

Watch this video to work out how to measure yourself for the correect size

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 5 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

Training Advice

We are now getting into some bigger training weeks.

The combination of longer weekend runs and either a tempo run or hill repeats sessions during the week is putting your body under more stress. If you are consistent with the stretches and exercises, and you are following the running program so that there are not any big jumps in volume, then your body should tolerate the increased load and you will become stronger and faster.

If you have a few niggles starting to appear that you are worried about, here are some strategies you should use to help keep them under control.

Adopt the “little and often” philosophy . Breaking your weekly distance into shorter but more regular runs will be easier for your body to cope with.

- In an ideal training program the long run is important, but it is counter-productive if you then have to miss 2-3 days of training because of it.

- For example – you could split the total volume of your long run between Saturday and Sunday, or Sunday and Monday – so that your overall weekly volume remains similar, but you don’t have the extra stress of a really long run for your body to cope with.

Speedwork – Don’t do any! Whether it is hill reps, tempo park runs or even hill reps. If you have got a niggle then leave any speed sessions out of your program until the niggle has settled.

- You will get a lot more benefit out of being able to continue to train than you will from persevering with speedwork and potentially making an injury worse.

Self Massage – sit down every evening and massage your sore bits (usually calves, feet, ITBs)

- A foam roller can be helpful for I TBs, quads and calves

- A tennis ball or golf ball can be useful for the sole of your foot (through the arch of your foot – not over the heel or the bony bits near the ball of your foot)

- A trigger point ball can be useful for your glute muscles

Ice – Icing a swollen achilles tendon, an inflamed ITB, or a painful foot can be a great way to help settle your symptoms in time to be able to run again the next day.

- Use ice cubes in a plastic bag NOT one of those blue gel packs. If ice cubes are not possible then frozen peas will (just) suffice. Ice cubes stay at a constant temperature (0 degrees) until they have melted. Ice packs usually start off too cold (-7 degrees) and warm up too quickly, so they can give you a nasty “freezer burn” and they don’t stay cold long enough to be effective.

Stretching – stretching your calf muscles for example can help to reduce the tension in your Achilles tendon. Stretching your glute muscles can help to reduce ITB and knee symptoms.

Most importantly – “Listen to your Body” – if you are concerned about a niggle or an injury during your training, then get it diagnosed by a trusted health care professional and take some proactive steps towards managing it and getting treatment if required.

Do not try and stick to the weekly km if you do have an issue. Continuing to push through pain when you have a problem could stop you turning up on race day.

Strength and Stability Workouts

This week we are stepping up to some harder strength and stability exercises. They are now 20 minute workouts and they include a kettlebell, skipping rope and you need a bench or a step for doing steps ups. We will also be adding some plyometric (jumping) exercises.

Try and get hold of a kettlebell that is somewhere between 2kg and 8kg (depending on your upper body strength) for these workouts.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Cadence

Cadence is the number of steps per minute you take. There is a bit of controversy around whether there is a specific number you should aim for. The “golden number” of 180 – is often quoted.

I am a huge believer that 180 is the gold standard and something that you should all ultimately be aiming for.

What should you do to improve your cadence?

The best way to work on improving your cadence is to use a metronome. You can buy a small, clip-on, digital metronome that is perfect for the purpose, or if you run with your phone, you can download a metronome app and use that. Set the metronome to the appropriate beat, and run in time with the beeps (one foot landing each time you hear a beep).

- We have digital metronomes available in our shop which are perfect for helping you regulate your cadence.

- A few watches now have built in metronomes – so check to see if your watch can be your metronome.

- There are a lot of free metronome Apps available for both Apple and Android phones which are also perfect for the job.

Follow these steps to make sure you do it accurately and safely

- Measure your cadence. During the middle of a normal training run, count your steps on one foot (i.e just your left) for a minute on a section of flat ground. Double it. This will give you your cadence. Repeat this several times over several runs to work out an accurate average.

- It is difficult to increase your cadence by more than 10 steps/minute in any one go. If your cadence is 160, for example, you should set your metronome to 170 and get used to that for a month, before increasing it further to 180.

- Continue using the metronome for as long as you need to until 180 becomes your natural / subconscious gait pattern.

There are two common, but temporary repercussions of increasing your cadence that you should be aware of

- It will increase your heart rate. Expect to breathe a bit harder, and get tired a bit quicker than you have been used to. Your cardio-vascular system will adjust over time, but expect it to take 2-3 months to fully adjust.

- Your calf muscles will probably do more work, and get tighter. As our stride gets shorter, our foot usually lands flatter, which uses the calf muscle more. Your calf muscles will get stronger with time, but some extra stretching and/or foam rolling will help during the transition.

I have been working as a physiotherapist treating running injuries for nearly thirty years, and I have spent the last sixteen years working with thousands of runners to improve their technique and reduce their injuries.

Cadence has been one of the most effective and beneficial changes most of those runners have made .

If you want to take your running to the next level, and you haven’t yet focused on your cadence, make sure you do. It can transform your running.

If you like running with music, it is possible to use an App to play music at a certain number of beats per minute. It is much harder though, to follow the rhythm of music than it is to follow the simple beat of a metronome, so I would highly recommend using a simple metronome App initially, and once you have become accustomed to the higher cadence and it feels natural, then you could switch back to running with music.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
An ongoing issue that athletes face is maintaining a strong immune system – especially when you are in a peak training phase. You need to make sure you are providing your body with the correct nutrition and resources to protect yourself from colds, flu’s and viruses.

Endurance running compromises the immune system as oxidative stress is increased; it is important to counter this with an increase in Anti Oxidant foods to counter the free radicals and restore balance. Reducing oxidative stress is also critical as it helps to protect damage to the mitochondria – the powerhouse of our energy production.

Key Anti Oxidant Nutrients:

Vitamin C, Vitamin E, Vitamin A and Co Q10

Antioxidant food sources:

- Capsicum, Broccoli, Dark Green Leafy Veg, Tomatoes, Sweet Potato

- Berries and Citrus Fruits, Papaya, Kiwi

- Green Tea and Matcha Tea

- Organ meats – Liver, heart

- Oily Fish – sardines, mackerel and salmon

- Nuts and Seeds

How many of these foods do you include on a daily basis?

You need to be aiming for a minimum of 5 serves of vegetables and 1-2 serves of fruit per day. Not only do you need the carbohydrate that they offer, but also the nutrient density. If you are struggling to include enough – smoothies are a great way to boost you intake. You could use fruit, vegetables, add in some matcha tea (powder) plus a handful of nuts or seeds.

If you don’t like the sound of organ meats, you can buy some mince meat that has it added, you won’t even know the difference! Or include a good quality pate into your regular diet.

Many athletes benefit from good quality antioxidant supplements, especially if your diet is lacking in these essential nutrients. Seek advice from a qualified nutritionist or naturopath regarding supplements to ensure that your investment is going to be of maximum benefit to you.

This week, I want you to consciously try and include 5 serves of vegetables a day. If you already doing this, then stick to it. If you are not currently eating 5 serves of veges per day then start trying. to improve it, so that your diet is complementing all of your training effort

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 6 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

We are building the volume again this week and adding in some Up/Down Repeats

We are introducing some Up Down repeats this week. The purpose of UpDown Repeats is to improve your skill and speed at downhill running, and to strengthen your quad muscles which will help you to climb strongly after the downhill sections of the course. For these reps find a 1km section of your run route (road or fire trail) which is consistently undulating. Ideally on gentle inclines of 5 to 8 degrees. Run these reps at tempo effort

(NB: your pace will vary significantly depending on whether you are running uphill or downhill, but your level of effort or perceived exertion should be consistent during the rep).

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
You should now be eating loads of veggies, have a system to monitor your food intake and be a vision of health! The next thing to think about is what to eat when, to ensure your body is getting exactly what it needs, when it most needs it.

This week we are going to focus on what to eat after training.

Your post training meal is vitally important to stimulate muscle glycogen replacement, protein synthesis and blunting of cortisol (so you don’t end up with Adrenal fatigue). Its needs to be consumed within 45mins post training.

If your session is a tough one – and greater than 60mins, it is vital that you get this meal right in order to get the most from your training and progress with your goals. This meal needs to contain carbohydrates and protein. The carbs refuel the glycogen and blunts cortisol production (both are vital for weight control) and the protein helps repair the muscles and supports the immune system.

The amount that you need to consume for this meal depends on your body weight, the amount of training you are doing, and your personal goals. As a rough guide you should be looking for around 1 gram of carbs per kilo of body weight, and around 1/3 rd of your body weight in protein.

So for example an athlete that weighs 60 kilos, would have 60grams of carbs and 20 grams of protein for this recovery meal. If your session has been an extended session – like a very long run – the need for carbohydrates increases, you might need 1.5-2grams of carbs per kilo of body weight. If the session is 60mins or less, aim for 40gms carb and 10-15 protein.

Choose good quality nutrient dense carbohydrates like fruit, starchy veg, wholegrains, legumes, nuts and seeds, and good quality protein such as eggs, fish, lean meat and dairy. This will ensure that your body is getting the nutrients it needs to have you in the best health possible on race day.

Post training breakfast might be:

- Fruit with Yoghurt, topped with nuts and Seeds or muesli

- Eggs and Toast – can add spinach or Avo

- Smoothie

- Frittata with potato/sweet potato, corn

- Porridge made with milk, topped with fruit, or yoghurt, drizzle honey

Post training dinner might be:

- Chicken Stir fry with Brown rice

- Steak with sweet potato and greens

- Grilled fish with buckwheat, beetroot and spinach salad

- Homemade hamburgers with a large leafy green side salad.

This week stick with all the great work you are doing and start experimenting with your post run meal. If you get a chance, mark down what you eat and note if you feel better the next day, so you start to get an idea of what works for you

notes.label: Gear
notes.text:
Your Shoes

With only 6 weeks until your race, if you are thinking of changing your shoes or getting new ones now would be a good time to get them. You ideally need to test them on 2 or 3 long runs to make sure they are comfortable and that they are not going to cause blisters.

Welcome to Week 7 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

We are increasing volume again this week.

It is VITAL, that you “listen to your body” and adjust your training volume and intensity according to how your body is coping. If, for example, you have a niggly knee or a calf muscle which is not coping well with the long run, you could:

- Split the long run into two separate runs For example, run 20km on Sunday and 10km on Monday. Although this is slightly less ideal than completing the long run, it will allow you to maintain the overall weekly volume, and minimise the risk of flaring up your knee or calf muscle injury.

- For example, run 20km on Sunday and 10km on Monday. Although this is slightly less ideal than completing the long run, it will allow you to maintain the overall weekly volume, and minimise the risk of flaring up your knee or calf muscle injury.

- Try Walking / Hiking instead of running You can usually still walk even when running has become uncomfortable or painful. If you think your body might not cope with the long run which is scheduled, then think about opting for the equivalent time walking/hiking instead.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Retesting your stability

If you have been following the program and completing the strength and stability workouts, then your stability should have improved. In week one, I got you to complete my one minute stability test and write down your score. Let’s test it again and see how you have improved.

Test your stability now

Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Count in seconds. 1, 2, 3…… How long did you last until you put your foot on the ground?

If you made it to

- less than 10… I don’t think you have been following the program!

- 10 – 30 ………. If better than before, then keep going

- 30 – 45 ………. Good

- 60 seconds – Great. Keep doing what you are doing

Record your score again. Hopefully. it has improved since week 1. If not, don’t worry. Just keep working away at the strength workouts and it should start to improve at some stage soon.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
At this stage of the training plan, you may be getting ravenous!

So this week we are going to cover how to increase your calories to meet training demands, and avoid weight gain.

As your training load starts to increase so does your energy demands. It is critical that you make sure your body is receiving the nutrients and hydration that it needs, so that you maintain the energy you need to train effectively and that your immune system is not compromised. Following the JERF principle will ensure you are consuming a nutrient dense diet, and now would also be a good time to re-cap what we have covered in the first few weeks of the plan – what are healthy carbs, protein and fat. Pay special attention to including protein at every meal, and hitting your daily protein target.

As your energy demands increase, your metabolism is firing, and you are allocating more time to training, – it is very easy to reach for packaged snacks and takeaway food, especially if you become “hangry” .. (hungry + angry ! ). Around this time of increased demand it is also very easy for some people to start putting on weight – even though you are training more. 80% of your weight is controlled by what you eat, only 20% is from exercise.

Now, more than ever, it is important to allocate time to food shopping, and preparation – you can’t out run a bad diet !

If you are prone to weight gain, or trying to lose some weight before your event, then timing your carbohydrate intake will be key. Your post training meal (recovery meal) should still contain some starchy carbs but all other meals should focus on quality protein, a small amount of healthy fat, with a large portion of “above the ground vegetables”.

Your homework this week – Stick with what you are doing. Keep a note of your food intake, eat lots of veggies and ideally track the amount of calories you are burning to ensure you are eating enough. Most running watches, along with My Fitness Pal, will give you an indication of the actual number of calories you are burning each day.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 8 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan – your second recovery week

Good news. This week is a recovery week in the 12 week program and there are only 4 weeks to go!

This week the the long run is shorter and the Thursday session is easier. By reducing the volume and intensity of the training this week, it will allow your body a chance to recover from the fatigue and tight muscles which will have been building up over the last three weeks.

The recovery week will set you up to be fresh and raring to go for the final phase of the program.

Despite the reduced running volume, this is NOT A REST WEEK .

You need to continue with the same number of runs per week and be just as diligent (if not, more so) with your body maintenance sessions. A week of complete rest will probably leave you feeling tired and sluggish and less motivated to get back into the training next week. The aim of the recovery week is to keep your body and your brain used to running, whilst still logging some all-important km’s in the training diary.

Try and do the 3 minute morning ritual every day this week. This will really help keep niggles at bay.

Rest and Sleep

Getting adequate sleep is an extremely important part of your training program. This is often overlooked when training for a specific event, especially when the training load increases – as extra training hours are often prioritised over sleep – this is not a good strategy and often ends up compromising the immune system or contributing to fatigue.

Your training program includes at least one rest day per week, it is vital that you allow your body rest – as this is when the muscles repair and re-build. Resting also allows hormones such as cortisol to recover and decrease – which is vital for weight management and ensuring that you do not suffer from over training syndrome.

Activities such as swimming, light yoga, having a sauna or getting a sports massage, are excellent choices for rest days.

If you struggle to fall asleep at night, try going to bed an hour earlier. Developing a pre-bedtime routine can also help, for example -2 hours prior to bed – finish eating and avoid screens, enjoy a cup of herbal tea, and read a book to calm your mind and help you fall asleep.

Most athletes need 7-8 hours sleep per night.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
This week we are covering daily hydration and how important this is as you increase the volume of training.

Water is the most abundant constituent of the body representing approximately 60% of your body weight. Water is essential to virtually every body function including digestion, absorption and transport of nutrients, elimination of body waste and regulation of body temperature, and many other chemical processes.

Dehydration will impact your performance during exercise, and leave you with a headache, fatigue, and a foggy brain !

So how much is enough each day ?

35ml per kilo of body weight i.e. 70kg x35 = 2450ml.

Don’t panic …. …Any fluids count towards your total including coffee and tea . You also absorb water through foods, especially fruit and vegetables many are 70-95 % water.

A good guide is to try and drink 6-8 glasses a day, (assume a glass = 450mls)

If you have two coffees (or tea) per day – they are about 250mls each, so there’s one glass done!

If you have trouble remembering to drink enough water get yourself some good quality, BPA free bottles, and carry them with you …. in the car, on the bus, at your desk, etc, Most of us spend lots of time driving, it’s a good time to rehydrate !

How can I tell if I am getting enough water?

Urine should be pale, straw colour. It is often slightly darker first thing in the morning, and becomes progressively lighter through the day if you are well hydrated. If urine is dark and has strong odour this is an indication that you are dehydrated.

What about when I Exercise?

During exercise you loose extra water through sweating and increased respiration. On average, you will loose 700ml – 850mls per hour of exercise.

Most people will not drink this amount DURING the exercise, so it is important to make up the difference throughout the day. Try to hydrate consistently throughout the day by regularly sipping water. (Rather than 3 glasses in the morning and 3 at night! )

Are Sports drinks a good choice for hydration?

Sports drinks contain water, electrolytes (generally sodium and potassium) and carbohydrates (sugar). The average 600ml bottle of sports drink contains the same amount of sugar as a soft drink!!

If you are trying to lose weight, sports drinks are not the best option for you.

If you are exercising for under 60mins you do not need a sports drink. Water is all you need.

Do I need to be replacing electrolytes?

If you are exercising 3-4 times per week for up to an hour at a time, you are most likely to be getting enough electrolytes from your diet.

If you are exercising for 90mins or longer 3-4 times per week, or training for an endurance event, you will need to start replacing electrolytes – sodium, potassium and magnesium. There are a variety of products on the market that enable this, without added sugar. Adding good quality salt to your food or water is also an easy way to replace some of the sodium lost.

notes.text:
Welcome to Week 9 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

This is the final big week in the program.

This week your long run should be all about putting into practise everything you have learnt.

Once again, you should be trying to find terrain which is similar to your race course. If you haven’t done a lot of downhill running in recent weeks, then this would be a good week to focus on the downhill sections during your long run.

When you run downhill, you use your quad muscles as a brake, which causes micro tears in the muscle cells, which in turn, causes DOMs (delayed onset of muscle soreness). When your bodies repair this micro trauma (by eating healthy food and getting enough sleep), the muscle cells actually become stronger for a 4 – 6 week period.

What this means is that if you schedule a hardish downhill running session 3 weeks out from race day, your quads will be strong on race day. You will be less likely to suffer from cramp and less likely to get knee or ITB pain if you condition your legs in this way.

Please note – if you already have aches and pains in your knees then ignore this extra downhill training advice. A flatter course at an easy pace will be much a much better option for your knees.

Mental Training

I think it is important to understand the role your mental stamina plays in training and racing for a 21km event.

Most of you will have reached a point in a race where you can no longer maintain your pace. It happens in 5km races, and it definitely happens in ultra marathons. In fact, it happens so frequently in ultra marathons that it has a name. “Hitting the wall”

How many of you have hit the so-called wall?

That point in a race where you feel exhausted: your legs are tired, your feet hurt and you feel like the only way that you’ll make it to the finish line without dying is to either slow down, walk, or maybe even crawl

I think there is a strong case to suggest that training our brains will make us faster. Long training runs and speed workouts help us mentally prepare our brains. They teach us that we can keep going even when tired.

On your next run I recommend thinking about some strategies you can use to keep going when the going gets tough.

Ideas like

- spend 1km thanking a single person that helped you make your race. Then someone else the next 1km and so on.

- sing your favourite song in your head to help stop any negative thoughts creeping in.

- Use the alphabet and starting at the letter A, think of a word about why you love trail running. For example, atmosphere, bananas, cheering …

notes.text:
Nutrition Guide for Race Day

It is important you know exactly what you are going to eat on race day and you have practiced this as part of your training. This will put your mind at ease and help you feel prepared. This week we will discuss race day nutrition that you can practice on this week’s long run.

What should you have for breakfast?

You may feel very nervous on race day morning. It is definitely not the time to consume anything new – (food or fluids) even if it is free, or your friend highly recommends it.

A light breakfast 2 hours prior to the race is ideal – it should be mostly carbohydrates, and around 1-2grams of carb per kilo of body weight.

Eg; if you weigh 60kgs, your breakfast should be 60-120 grams of carbohydrates. If you don’t have much time before the race, stick to the lower end of this scale.

The meal should be low in fibre, low in fat and low in protein, to decrease the risk of gastric upset.

Eg: Banana, White bread, crumpets, honey, fruit juice, sports bar.

30 Grams of carbs :

- 1 medium banana

- 2 slices white bread

- 1.5 crumpets

- 4-6 dates

- 2 Tbs honey

- 1 gel (check label, usually 20-30gms)

- Sports Drink – check label

It is not advisable that you drink sports drink for the hour before the race. Just have your breakfast, and then sip on water. Just prior to the start (i.e. 10-15 mins) you can have a gel if you like.

Fuelling during the race:

By race day you should have practiced a fuelling strategy, and know exactly what your race day nutrition plan is. Do not leave it until the night before the race to figure out, or worse still – “wing it” on the day.

Hydration

This is an extremely important part of your nutrition strategy that is often overlooked.

The amount of water you lose during a race is very individual and also dependent on the weather. Ideally you will have already calculated your hourly sweat rate, and know how much you lose. If you don’t know your sweat rate – a guideline is around 600 -750mls per hour for most people.

Faster runners will struggle to get this amount in over the course of the race, but it is vital not to become dehydrated. Try to have a small drink at all of the aid stations throughout the race.

Slower runners are generally better at consuming water during the race, and hence the issue of hyponatremia needs to be considered. This is when the level of sodium in your blood is too low and your body can no longer regulate the amount of water in your cells. To overcome this, you need to consume sodium (and other electrolytes) during the race, and be sure not to “over hydrate”.

After run recovery

You should pay some attention to what you eat in the 45-60 minute period immediately after you run

You need to replenish glycogen stores (carbohydrates), plus some protein for muscle recovery. This should be in the ratio 4:1 Carb:Protein

Sports recovery drinks/bars designed for this are great in a race situation as they are very portable and you may not have access to your regular recovery meal, or you may not like what is available at the finish line.

notes.text:
Welcome to Week 10 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

It is taper time!

It is now time to start backing off the training volume, but it is important to try and maintain the same training frequency and pace / intensity. The idea with tapering down to an event is to freshen your legs, boost your immune system and regain some energy. However, if you stop running completely you might end up feeling “flat” and underperforming on race day.

Overcooked or Undercooked on Race Day – Which is better?

Overcooked = slightly overtrained and possibly a little under your “ideal” race weight. Undercooked = slightly undertrained and possibly a kilogram or two over your “ideal” race weight.

If you were to ask me whether or not you would be better to be overcooked or undercooked for any endurance race, my answer would always be undercooked . (NB: unless you are using it as a build up race for an upcoming longer event).

Going into a long trail event undercooked doesn’t mean taking the soft/easy option and opting out of the long, hard training sessions you have planned. Nor does it mean sleeping through your alarm clock on a regular basis because you “don’t feel like training” on that particular morning.

If you are an experienced campaigner and have been racing ultras for a long time, then you will probably feel that you know what works best for you in terms of a taper. If that is the case, and you a racing to a level you are happy with, then you should stick with what you know.

If you have done a few long trail events and feel like you have trained well, but haven’t yet had a race that you are completely happy with, then you may have got the taper wrong.

If you are new to trail running and you are not sure what to do for these last few weeks, then avoid the temptation to squeeze in “one last hard session”. It is more likely to be for mental reassurance than physical conditioning that you feel like you should do it. You are unlikely to get any fitter in the final 3 weeks, but you do have a high chance of becoming more fatigued, or worse still, injured, if you try and keep up the high volume work right through until race day.

Tapering: How to manage your last 3 weeks of training

The final 3 weeks are all about keeping your legs ticking over, keeping your brain happy that you still know how to run, and also keeping with the routine that your body has become accustomed to over the last few months of training.

If, for example, you are used to getting up at 5am most mornings to run, and with 3 weeks to go you suddenly change to “sleeping in” until 6:30am every morning, then your body is going to wonder what you are doing to it. It will probably throw your digestive system, and possibly your general motivation out of kilter and by race day you may not feel like you are “ready” to race.

It is a better idea with 3 weeks to go to maintain your frequency of running, but back off the volume. If, for example, you have been following the training plan and running 4-5 days per week, then you should continue to run 4-5 days per week

- With 3 weeks to go you reduce the total weekly volume down to about 70% of the biggest week

- With 2 weeks to go it reduces further to 45-50% of the biggest week

- In the final week , two easy 5km aerobic runs is great for the brain and not taxing on the legs.

None of these runs should be faster (or slower) than usual either. There is a common mentality in runners that their short runs need to be faster. This is certainly not the case during your taper weeks. Keep to your normal training pace and try to enjoy the fact that you have more energy than you have had recently.

Following these basic guidelines will go a long way towards ensuring you are not overcooked on race day.

Try to enjoy your taper. It is a time when a lot of people start second-guessing everything they have done:

- “Should I just do one more long run?”

- “I wish I’d done that 4 hour run my friends did a few weeks ago”

- “Should I try out that different high-carb drink that John recommended yesterday?”

- Will thicker socks be better for a long race?”

Putting it bluntly, it is too late now to change anything . What is done is done, and more importantly, what is not done – you can’t catch up on.

Enjoy your taper and give it everything you’ve got on a fresh set of legs on race day.

Get More Sleep

One of the best ways to help your body recover from the past few weeks of heavy training is to sleep more. Research shows that athletic performance improves with sufficient sleep. Rested athletes are faster. Get whatever extra sleep you can over the next 3 weeks. 30 minutes here, and 30 minutes there all counts. So sleep when you can.

notes.text:
With race day now 3 weeks away you should still be practicing your race day nutrition strategy on your last few weekend runs. It helps to write down the source of fuel, how many carbs it contains and then how much you need based on your goal time.

Think about how you are going to carry your fuel on race day, and practice this in training. There is a lot of mandatory gear you need to carry so make sure you have a system in place for accessing your nutrition at the right time on race day.

Have a plan, but be flexible. – try to stick to your nutrition plan that you have practiced in training. However, if you start to feel sick during the race, back off the fuel and sip water for then next 20-30 mins and then try to eat again.

notes.text:
Welcome to Week 11 of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

More tapering to look forward to this week.

This week sees a significant reduction in the length of the long run, and a “fairly easy” mid-week hill repeats session. The other runs remain unchanged.

By maintaining both the frequency and intensity of the runs, but dropping the total volume, it will give your legs a chance to recover from the hard training over the past 10 weeks, whilst at the same time keeping them used to ticking over. This tapering effect will also allow your immune system and overall energy levels to improve, which will have you fresh and raring to go on race day.

It is not too late to get more sleep

One of the best ways to help your body recover from the past few weeks of heavy training is to sleep more. Research shows that athletic performance improves with sufficient sleep. Rested athletes are faster. Get whatever extra sleep you can over the next 2 weeks. 30 minutes here, and 30 minutes there all counts. So sleep when you can.

Read this great ARTICLE from Runners World explaining why extra sleep in the week before your major race will pay dividends on race day.

Your Body Maintenance

You still need to keep up with your stretching and rolling routine this week. It is easy to get a bit slack with body maintenance as the training volume decreases, but it is just as important as ever. You need your muscles to be in tip-top shape on race day.

This week we are dropping back to the 10 minute workouts to help maintain your stability and complement the taper.

notes.text:
How to manage your nutrition through your taper

As you head towards race day your total training load is decreasing. This can be a difficult time, and many people experience “taper tantrums”. Your metabolism with still be working well, and even though you are not burning as many calories in training, you will most likely find that you are still eating the same volume of food.

It is vital that you stick with the “JERF” principle at this point as you do not want to compromise your immune system. Many people feel like they are ‘getting a cold” during taper week – it is often just imaginary !! – you have put so much work into getting to this point, it is normal to feel anxious about things that could set you back or impact your performance.

If you are prone to weight gain, this is a good week to watch your carb intake closely, and focus on mostly above the ground vegetables, lean protein and healthy fats.

notes.text:
Welcome to Week 12. The final week of your Bouddi 21km Training Plan

Congratulations on making it this far through the training program. All of the hard work is done, and this weekend you get to reap the rewards of all of that effort.

Training Advice

With only one week to go your legs should be feeling fresher and stronger, but you’re probably starting to question everything:

- Why are my calves so tight?

- Am I getting a cold?

- Have I done enough training?

- Dave thinks I should have gels instead of bars, I wonder if he’s right . . .

All of these questions and insecurities are a normal part of tapering. You have to trust in what you have done . And, if you haven’t done it, it is too late anyway – so there is no point in fretting about it.

Strength and Stability

This week we are dropping the strength and stability work, but maintaining the stretching and rolling.

The focus is on maintaining flexibility and mobility to help prevent your joints and muscles stiffening up over the course of this week. The reduction in training, and change in routine, can have a negative impact on your body, so it is very important to keep up with this mobility training.

NB: For any of you following the program who haven’t been doing these stretches and exercises regularly – DON’T START NOW! – Think of it like running training. If you haven’t started your running training yet, then you can’t cram it all into the final week. If you haven’t started stretching or rolling yet, then you definitely shouldn’t try to cram it all into the last week. You will do yourself far more harm than good.

Good Luck – I hope you have a great race

Preparing for race day

Do you need to carb load this week?

For long distance trail events it is beneficial to “carb load” for 3-4 days prior to the race to ensure that the glycogen stores in your muscles are full and ready to power your over the 21 km distance. This will help to delay the onset of fatigue.

This does not meaning increasing meal size, or calories, but ensuring that each meal does contain predominately carbohydrates, along with a small amount of protein and healthy fat. Vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains are excellent sources of carbohydrates. You may find your weight increases over these few days, as carbohydrates store extra water in your cells – don’t worry, you’ll need the extra water on race day.

Top 5 Tips For Carb Loading

1. Once you are in taper mode, you are effectively carb loading as your body isn’t burning as much due to reduced training load

2. For the 3- 4 days prior to the event you can increase your carbohydrate intake by changing your ratio of Carbs: Protein for your meals, but keep total calories the same. For example, instead of chicken and Veggies, opt for risotto with veggies, or pasta with veggies, or cut back the chicken portion and add more starchy veg such as sweet potato, potato or beetroot.

3. The day before your event, have a bigger lunch and smaller dinner than you usually would, this allows time for digestion. Include an extra piece of fruit or starchy veg in your day – banana/pear/apple/potato/sweet potato

4. Stick to simple, good quality “plain” food the day before – it’s not the time to be super healthy with brown rice, beans and lentils… nor the day to have a spicy Indian Curry.. keep it simple and low fibre.

5. Carbohydrates hold 3-4 times their weight in water, so don’t over do the carb loading (if you’re not used to eating lots of carbs) or you risk standing on the start line feeling heavy and bloated.

Should you drink extra water?

Yes. Hydration levels are critical for athletes, and you should arrive at the race fully hydrated. You should be drinking 2 litres of water a day for 3 days prior to your race, adding a few pinches of salt will help increase the uptake of water into the cells. You can also use electrolyte replacement tablets to help increase hydration levels.

To overcome this, you need to consume sodium (and other electrolytes) during the race, and be sure not to “over hydrate”.

If you are still of sound mind in the aftermath of your race, and you want to ensure that you recover from it quickly, you should pay some attention to what you eat in the 45-60 minute period immediately after the race, ideally before you reach for your first beer!

Have a member of your support crew bring something along for you to have at the completion of the race.

Alcohol is not a good source of hydration. Make sure you hydrate and re-fuel properly before celebrations begin!

glossary.definition:
This program is designed for runners who have a solid base of consistent training but are new to trail running or stepping up to the half marathon distance. You should be running around 20–25km each week and able to complete a long run of 8–10km comfortably. The plan builds gradually, focusing on endurance, strength, and confidence over mixed terrain. You’ll complete longer weekend runs, mid-week intervals, and trail-specific mobility and strength work to help you prepare for race day without injury.

Beginner runners are aiming to complete the 21km course feeling strong and well-prepared.

This program is ideal for runners who have been training consistently for at least 6 months and are ready to push themselves toward a stronger finish. You should be running 35–40km per week and comfortable completing long runs of up to 12km. The program includes a mix of endurance runs, speed sessions, hill work, and race-specific trail running to develop both strength and stamina. Recovery and mobility work are also built into the plan to keep you training consistently.

Intermediate runners are aiming to run a steady race from start to finish, with confidence on the climbs and descents.

This plan is built for experienced trail runners looking to perform at their best on race day. You should be running 50km or more per week across a range of terrains and able to handle long runs of 12–14km comfortably. The plan includes race-specific sessions to fine-tune your pacing, fitness, and technical skills—plus advanced strength and mobility routines to reduce injury risk and support high-performance training.

Advanced runners are aiming to race the 21km course with a consistently hard effort and strong technical execution.

This chart shows the long run distance and total weekly volume for each of the three levels. It can help you to choose which level of the plan is the most appropriate one to follow. It will also help you plan your long runs in advance.

Choose the level that suits your current level of fitness. e.g. if you have consistently been running 15-20km per week for the past few months then choose the beginner level. The intermediate and advanced plans will probably cause you an injury. You can always change levels during the plan if you are finding it too easy or too hard.

Session Descriptions (in alphabetical order)

Accelerations are 20 to 40 second efforts building from an easy jog to a relaxed hard effort, and then easing back down to a jog again. Focus on running tall and keeping your cadence high and your strides short. Slowly walk or jog for 1 minute between accelerations. The purpose of accelerations is improve your leg speed, hip mobility, glute strength and running technique. NB: They are not a sprinting or speedwork session.

You should be able to talk comfortably in normal sentences when running at an aerobic pace. The purpose of these sessions is to add more mileage to your week without causing too much fatigue. Aerobic runs improve your running economy to make you a more efficient runner.

A routine of exercises including stretching, stability, strengthening, foam rolling and trigger point ball. There will be regular changes to the exercises included in the routine, to focus on different body parts as required to compliment the training program. NB: These exercises are an integral part of this training program. The Body Maintenance sessions are equally as important as the running sessions.

Cross training could be swimming, cycling, elliptical, rowing, pilates or yoga or a low impact gym class. These sessions are good for your body as they use different muscle groups and are low impact. They will help to increase your aerobic fitness and endurance without the impact of increasing your running mileage. Don’t perform these sessions if you are feeling too fatigued from the current training load.

Cross training sessions can be anything from 30 mins to 90 mins in duration.

These elevation profiles are a measure of the total amount of vertical elevation during a run. Your total elevation can be measured by most current GPS watches, or you can run with your phone and download an app called Strava which will record your elevation. NB: The ELEV figures in this program are guidelines, they do not have to be adhered to exactly.

The Bouddi 21k course has an official elevation of 775m. The elevation targets in the plan are set at approximately 200m of vert per 10km of running for beginner level, 300m of vert per 10km of running for intermediate level and 400m of vert per 10km of running for advanced level.

If you are feeling excessively tired or you are finding the training difficult, you should stick to the lower end of the vert targets, or even reduce them further. You will get more benefit from reducing the vert, but maintaining as much of the training volume as you can in order to reduce injury risk and keep your body healthy.

Pick a relatively flat course for these runs. Including a few small hills is ok. Something like 100m / 10km of running. The purpose of these flatter runs is active recovery. They help to increase your weekly mileage safely, without causing too much fatigue on your system.

Hill repeats are repeated short segments of harder uphill running. They increase aerobic power, high-intensity fatigue resistance, pain tolerance, and run-specific strength. The ideal hill on which to run hill repeats is a steady, moderate gradient of 4 to 6 percent and about 500m long. NB: During hill repeats you should be breathing hard and only able to speak 2 or 3 words at a time. BUT YOU ARE NOT SPRINTING!

I suggest you make as many of your long runs as possible on trail. Trail running is more forgiving on your body due to the variation in your stride pattern caused by the changing terrain. You are also training for a trail event, so training on trails is more race-specific.

In an ideal world you should try to make most of your long runs on terrain that is similar to the course you will be racing on. This will help to condition your legs for race day, and will also give you the opportunity to practice using poles if you are intending to race with them.

Go to www.parkrun.com.au to learn more about Park Runs. You can replace a park run with a 5km run on the flat or small rolling hills if there isn’t a convenient park run near you, or if you prefer to run alone.

During the recovery weeks all of the runs are at aerobic pace and there is significantly less total elevation for the week. We continue with some easy accelerations during the recovery week to help maintain your leg speed and running confidence. The purpose of a recovery week is to let your body and your immune system recover. It will also help to reduce any muscle tightness and niggles. These weeks will help to restore your energy for the next training build phase. Do Not do any of these runs fast, and Please Do Not run over the stated volumes.

Rest days are vital to help your body recover from the training sessions. Without adequate rest you are more likely to become ill and injured. Try to get as much sleep and recovery time as possible on these days.

Rolling hills is the term we use to describe running over a course that is consistently going up and downhill for the duration of your run. Plan ahead and identify a course that has a good amount of up and downhill. The hills should be as regular as possible throughout the course. Consider running a short hilly loop multiple times if you don’t have access to a long hilly route. You should average approximately 200m – 400m of vertical elevation per 10km of running on rolling hills.

Find the longest staircase that you can conveniently get to for this session. The more steps the better. For these stair repeats you should be mostly hiking. You can run small sections of them if you are feeling strong, but hiking will be more race-specific. Run slowly back down the stairs slowly to recover. Repeat for the stated duration on the training plan. NB: Your pace should stay consistent throughout the session. Don’t start so fast that you can’t maintain your pace.

You should be able to talk in short sentences or a few words at a time while running at tempo pace . Think about running between 10km and half marathon race pace. The purpose of the tempo sessions is to help improve your running form, your VO2Max, and to help to keep your hips and glutes mobile and strong.

The purpose of UpDown Repeats is to improve your skill and speed at downhill running, and to strengthen your quad muscles which will help you to climb strongly after the downhill sections of the course. For these reps find a 1km section of your run route (road or fire trail) which is consistently undulating. Ideally on gentle inclines of 5 to 8 degrees. Run these reps at tempo effort (NB: your pace will vary significantly depending on whether you are running uphill or downhill, but your level of effort or perceived exertion should be consistent during the rep. For the recovery between reps you should either walk or jog slowly for 2 minutes (meaning your next rep might be in the reverse direction depending on the course you have chosen).

The main focus of this long run is the uphill sections of the course. During the second half of this run, run up the hills at tempo effort (able to talk in 3 – 4 word sentences before needing to draw breath). The purpose of this session is to increase cardio-vascular fitness, glute and calf muscle strength and improve your fatigue resistance and mental strength for race day.
